What Does Olsun Mean in Turkish? The -sın Ending Behind Everyday Wishes

Seda Sürel
5 days ago
6 min read

For readers in a hurry: Olsun means "may it be." It is ol- (to be) plus the ending -sın / -sin / -sun / -sün, the third-person form of the Turkish imperative and the same ending sits inside kolay gelsin, geçmiş olsun, afiyet olsun and hayırlı olsun. Once you can see it, a list of phrases you memorized one by one becomes a single pattern and the same pattern will be waiting for you in a café, where the waiter uses it to bring your tea. Read on for how it works and where it stops working.


Spend an ordinary day in Türkiye with your ears open and the same small ending keeps coming back. A man carrying boxes up the stairs hears kolay gelsin from a neighbor. Someone back from the dentist hears geçmiş olsun. A plate lands on the table with afiyet olsun, and a friend holding the keys to a new flat waits for you to say hayırlı olsun.


A phrasebook lists these as four separate entries, each with its own translation. All four end in a verb carrying the same suffix.



The ending itself


Take a verb stem and add -sIn. Grammar books write it with a capital I because its vowel follows four-way vowel harmony, the same way the accusative ending does:


kal → kalsın (let it stay)

gel → gelsin (let it come)

ol → olsun (let it be)

gör → görsün (let him or her see)


The last vowel of the stem decides the form. After a or ı you get -sın, after e or i -sin, after o or u -sun, and after ö or ü -sün.


Turkish school grammar files this under emir kipi, the imperative, as its third-person form. Gerjan van Schaaik's Oxford Turkish Grammar gives it a chapter of its own under the name indirect imperative. Gel! is addressed to the person in front of you.


Gelsin points past the listener, toward someone or something else: let him come, have her come, may it come.


The form also does everyday work. In a tea garden you can order with İki çay gelsin, literally "let two teas come." A manager can say Ayşe Hanım gelsin and mean "send Ayşe Hanım in." A host can ask Çay gelsin mi?, offering to have tea brought.


When the "someone or something else" is a task, an illness or a meal, the same request becomes a wish. Kolay gelsin wishes that the work in front of someone comes easily. The cultural side of that phrase, and who says it to whom, is in The Quiet Ethics of Turkish: Understanding Kolay Gelsin.



Why olsun turns up everywhere


Olsun is ol-, the stem of olmak (to be, to become), plus the same ending: ol + sun. If olmak still feels slippery, the post on how "to be" works in Turkish covers it. As a wish, olsun means "may it be," and Turkish can place a noun, an adjective or a whole phrase in front of it.


Afiyet olsun – may it be with good health; said over food. (more on afiyet olsun)

Hayırlı olsun – may it be auspicious; for a new home, a new job, a new car.

Geçmiş olsun – may it be in the past; for an illness, an accident, a hard week. Geçmiş is the participle of geçmek, "to pass." (more on geçmiş olsun)

Sıhhatler olsun – may it bring good health; a traditional wish after a haircut or a bath. Yolun açık olsun – may your road be open; before a trip or a new undertaking.

Allah razı olsun – may God be pleased with you; a deep thank-you.


Başın sağ olsun belongs on this list too, with a warning attached. Literally "may your head be sound," it is said only to someone who has lost a person close to them. The grammar is identical to afiyet olsun, and the two sentences belong to completely different days. The usual reply is Dostlar sağ olsun, "may friends be well," which is one more olsun. The customs around the phrase are in Başın Sağ Olsun: What Turkish Holds in a House of Mourning.


Olsun can also stand alone. Said on its own, it keeps its literal sense, "let it be," and works like English "never mind" or "that's fine": someone says Geç kaldım ("I'm late") and the answer is Olsun, otur ("Never mind, sit down").



The same ending on other verbs


Olsun gets most of the attention, but any verb can take the ending:


Günün güzel geçsin. – May your day pass well. (Have a nice day.)

Allah şifa versin. – May God give healing.

Allah göstermesin. – May God not show it. (God forbid.)

Nazar değmesin. – May the evil eye not touch it.


The last two are negative. The negative suffix -mA comes between the stem and the ending: değ + me + sin → değmesin, ol + ma + sın → olmasın. After an apology you may hear Bir daha olmasın, "let it not happen again," usually a mild warning that also ends the subject.


When the wish is addressed to God, the third person is built into the sentence, because Allah is the subject: Allah gives; Allah does not show.



Blessing someone who isn't there


The third-person form also lets you bless someone who is absent. Compare the forms of the same verb:


Sağ ol. – thanks (to one person; literally "be well")

Sağ olun. – thanks (polite or plural)

Sağ olsun. – bless him or her (about someone else)

Sağ olsunlar. – bless them


Komşumuz sağ olsun, kapıyı açtı means "Our neighbor, bless him, opened the door for us." You are thanking a person who is not there to hear it. Sağ olsunlar, çok yardım ettiler does the same for a whole group. In the same way, Annen çabuk iyileşsin wishes a quick recovery to your friend's mother, who is not in the conversation.



Making your own wishes


The pattern is productive, so you can build wishes nobody taught you:


Sınavın iyi geçsin. – May your exam go well.

Yolculuğun rahat geçsin. – May your trip be comfortable.

Her şey gönlünce olsun. – May everything be as you wish.

Hafta sonun güzel geçsin. – Have a nice weekend.


A wish can be grammatically perfect and still sound odd, because the fixed formulas come attached to their situations and a translation will not tell you which situation that is. A 2009 study in the Canadian Journal of Applied Linguistics compared 23 common Turkish good-wish formulas with their French counterparts and found a perfect match for only one of them.



Where the pattern stops


Several everyday Turkish wishes use other structures, and they are easier to remember once you can name them.


Eline sağlık is a noun phrase with no verb at all: el (hand) + -ine + sağlık (health), "health to your hand," said to someone who has cooked or made something. The cook usually answers with afiyet olsun, so the exchange ends on an olsun after all.


Güle güle kullan is a second-person imperative: "use it laughing," said to someone with a new purchase.


İyi şanslar and başarılar are plural nouns, "good lucks" and "successes."


Keşke gelse expresses a different kind of wish, a longing for something that is not happening. It uses the conditional -sa / -se and means "if only he would come."

Then there is the sneeze. Çok yaşa, "live long," is a second-person imperative too, aimed straight at the person who sneezed, and the reply turns it around: Sen de gör, "may you see it too."



Vocabulary


kolay gelsin – may it come easy (said to someone working)

geçmiş olsun – may it be in the past; get well soon

afiyet olsun – enjoy your meal

hayırlı olsun – may it be auspicious; congratulations on something new

başın sağ olsun – my condolences

dostlar sağ olsun – reply to condolences

nazar değmesin – may the evil eye not touch it

Allah göstermesin – God forbid

sağ olsun – bless him / her (about someone absent)


 

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)


Q: What does olsun mean in Turkish?

A: Olsun means "may it be" or "let it be." It is ol-, the stem of olmak (to be), plus the third-person imperative ending -sun, and it appears in many everyday wishes such as afiyet olsun and geçmiş olsun. On its own, olsun can also mean "never mind" or "that's fine."


Q: What does -sin mean in Turkish?

A: In forms like gelsin and olsun, -sin is the third-person imperative ending, written -sIn in grammar books because its vowel changes with vowel harmony (-sın, -sin, -sun, -sün). It can mean "let him / her / it…" or, in wishes, "may…".


Q: Why is it olsun and not olsin?

A: The ending follows four-way vowel harmony. The stem ol- has the vowel o, so the suffix becomes -sun.


Q: What is the difference between gelsin and keşke gelse?

A: Gelsin presents his coming as something requested or wished for: let him come, may it come. Keşke gelse uses the conditional and expresses longing about something that is not happening: if only he would come.


Q: Can I invent my own wishes with -sin?

A: Yes. Sınavın iyi geçsin and günün güzel geçsin are natural Turkish. Fixed formulas such as başın sağ olsun belong to specific situations, so learn those together with the moment they are used.


For more on how suffixes build meaning, read Turkish grammar explained through structure, suffixes and sentence logic. For the opposite of a blessing, see the idiom ah etmek. If you want to practice these forms in conversation, you can book a lesson.

October 30, 2026

Building an Internal Developer Platform on Top of Kubernetes

How to turn Kubernetes into a self-service platform where developers ship services, databases, and dashboards without writing YAML

By Tom Jose | DevOps

10 min read

  • 1 Why Kubernetes Alone Isn't a Developer Platform
  • 2 Designing the Internal Developer Platform Architecture
  • 3 Building a Self-Service Developer Portal
  • 4 GitOps as the Deployment Engine
  • 5 Self-Service Infrastructure with Crossplane
  • 6 Golden Paths and Standardized Application Templates
  • 7 Security, RBAC, and Multi-Tenancy
  • 8 Observability and Day-2 Operations
  • 9 Common IDP Mistakes and Measuring Success
  • 10 IDP readiness checklist

Count the files a developer has to touch to ship a brand-new service on your Kubernetes platform. On most clusters I review, the answer lands between 12 and 20. A Deployment, a Service, an Ingress, an HPA, a ServiceAccount, an IAM role, a Terraform module for the database, an ExternalSecret, a ServiceMonitor, a GitHub Actions workflow, an Argo CD Application, and then a Jira ticket to the platform team for whatever's left.

Almost none of those files describe the service. They describe the infrastructure around it. Developers end up copying manifests from a neighbouring repo, changing the names, and hoping. Six months later you have forty services with forty slightly different ways of doing health checks.

This article walks through an Internal Developer Platform (IDP) built from Backstage, Argo CD, and Crossplane on EKS. In it, a developer goes from "I need a new service with a Postgres database" to a running, monitored deployment without writing a Kubernetes manifest or opening the AWS console. It's an architecture article, so there are no installation steps.

Why Kubernetes Alone Isn't a Developer Platform

Kubernetes gives you primitives: Pods, Services, volumes, RBAC. Primitives are what you build a platform from. They aren't a platform themselves. Handing raw Kubernetes to product teams creates three problems that get worse as you grow.

The first is cognitive load. A developer who wants to add a queue consumer shouldn't need to understand IRSA trust policies or why maxUnavailable: 0 matters during a rollout. Every hour spent on that is an hour not spent on the product.

The second is inconsistency. When every team writes its own manifests, every team makes its own mistakes. One service has no resource requests, another runs as root, a third has no PodDisruptionBudget. You find out which one during an incident.

The third is the ticket queue. Infrastructure that Kubernetes can't provision (databases, buckets, IAM) usually goes through the platform team. The team becomes a bottleneck, so developers wait days for an RDS instance that Terraform creates in eight minutes.

An IDP fixes all three by changing what developers interact with. They stop working with infrastructure and start working with products the platform team builds: a service template, a database API, a deployment workflow. The YAML still exists. It just moves to the people whose job is maintaining it.

Designing the Internal Developer Platform Architecture

Here's the architecture this article builds. Each layer has one job, and developers only touch the top one.

The design principle that matters most is that Git is the only write path. Backstage never calls the Kubernetes API or AWS directly. It creates repositories and opens pull requests. Argo CD reconciles what's in Git, and Crossplane reconciles cloud resources from Kubernetes objects that Argo CD applied.

That means every change, including "create a database," is reviewable, auditable, and revertable with the same tools. It also means Backstage can go down without taking deployments with it. The portal is a front door, not a dependency.

Building a Self-Service Developer Portal

Backstage does three jobs in this setup. The service catalog answers "who owns this and where does it run." TechDocs keeps documentation next to the code. Software templates create new things. The templates are where the self-service happens.

A template is a form plus a sequence of actions. Here's a trimmed version of the golden path template for a Go service with an optional database:

apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: go-service
  title: Go Service (recommended)
  description: HTTP service with CI, GitOps deployment, monitoring, and optional Postgres
  tags: [go, recommended]
spec:
  owner: group:platform-team
  type: service
  parameters:
    - title: Service details
      required: [name, owner]
      properties:
        name:
          title: Service name
          type: string
          pattern: '^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{2,30}$'
        owner:
          title: Owning team
          type: string
          ui:field: OwnerPicker
          ui:options:
            catalogFilter:
              kind: Group
        database:
          title: Postgres database
          type: string
          enum: [none, small, medium]
          default: none
  steps:
    - id: fetch-service
      name: Generate service code
      action: fetch:template
      input:
        url: ./skeleton
        values:
          name: ${{ parameters.name }}
          owner: ${{ parameters.owner }}
    - id: publish
      name: Create GitHub repository
      action: publish:github
      input:
        repoUrl: github.com?owner=payflow-eng&repo=${{ parameters.name }}
        defaultBranch: main
        protectDefaultBranch: true
    - id: fetch-gitops
      name: Generate deployment config
      action: fetch:template
      input:
        url: ./gitops
        targetPath: ./gitops
        values:
          name: ${{ parameters.name }}
          owner: ${{ parameters.owner }}
          database: ${{ parameters.database }}
    - id: gitops-pr
      name: Open GitOps pull request
      action: publish:github:pull-request
      input:
        repoUrl: github.com?owner=payflow-eng&repo=platform-gitops
        branchName: onboard-${{ parameters.name }}
        title: "Onboard ${{ parameters.name }}"
        description: Generated by the go-service template
        sourcePath: ./gitops
        targetPath: apps/${{ parameters.name }}
    - id: register
      name: Register in catalog
      action: catalog:register
      input:
        repoContentsUrl: ${{ steps['publish'].output.repoContentsUrl }}
        catalogInfoPath: /catalog-info.yaml
  output:
    links:
      - title: Repository
        url: ${{ steps['publish'].output.remoteUrl }}
      - title: Deployment pull request
        url: ${{ steps['gitops-pr'].output.remoteUrl }}

        repoContentsUrl: ${{ steps['publish'].output.repoContentsUrl }}
        catalogInfoPath: /catalog-info.yaml
  output:
    links:
      - title: Repository
        url: ${{ steps['publish'].output.remoteUrl }}
      - title: Deployment pull request
        url: ${{ steps['gitops-pr'].output.remoteUrl }}

The developer fills in three fields. The template creates the repository, opens the deployment PR, and registers the service in the catalog with its owner attached.

Notice the database field is an enum with three values, not a free-text instance class. That's deliberate, and it comes back in the Crossplane section.

GitOps as the Deployment Engine

Argo CD is the deployment engine, and the platform-gitops repository is its single source of truth. The layout is boring on purpose:

platform-gitops/
  apps/
    invoice-service/
      envs/
        staging/values.yaml
        production/values.yaml
    ledger-api/
      envs/
        staging/values.yaml
        production/values.yaml
platform-gitops/
  apps/
    invoice-service/
      envs/
        staging/values.yaml
        production/values.yaml
    ledger-api/
      envs/
        staging/values.yaml
        production/values.yaml

One ApplicationSet turns every apps/*/envs/* directory into an Argo CD Application, so onboarding a service means merging a PR. Nobody writes an Application by hand:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: services
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  goTemplate: true
  goTemplateOptions: ["missingkey=error"]
  generators:
    - git:
        repoURL: https://github.com/payflow-eng/platform-gitops.git
        revision: main
        directories:
          - path: apps/*/envs/*
  syncPolicy:
    preserveResourcesOnDeletion: true
  template:
    metadata:
      name: '{{index .path.segments 1}}-{{.path.basename}}'
    spec:
      project: services
      sources:
        - repoURL: https://github.com/payflow-eng/platform-charts.git
          targetRevision: service-chart-2.4.1
          path: charts/service
          helm:
            valueFiles:
              - $values/{{.path.path}}/values.yaml
        - repoURL: https://github.com/payflow-eng/platform-gitops.git
          targetRevision: main
          ref: values
      destination:
        name: 'eks-{{.path.basename}}'
        namespace: '{{index .path.segments 1}}'
      syncPolicy:
        automated:
          prune: true
          selfHeal: true
        syncOptions:
          - CreateNamespace=true

Each environment maps to a cluster (eks-staging, eks-production) registered in Argo CD. CI in the service repo builds the image, pushes it to ECR, and opens a PR that bumps the tag in staging/values.yaml. Promotion to production is another PR that copies the same tag forward. Git history becomes the deployment log.

Here's the sharp edge almost nobody plans for. That ApplicationSet also deploys the service's PostgresDatabase object. If someone deletes apps/invoice-service/ in a cleanup PR, the default behavior cascades: the Application is deleted, its resources are pruned, Crossplane sees the database object disappear, and it deletes the RDS instance. That's why preserveResourcesOnDeletion: true is in the manifest above. The Crossplane section adds a second safeguard, because one layer of protection on production data isn't enough.

Self-Service Infrastructure with Crossplane

Crossplane lets the platform team define its own Kubernetes APIs for cloud infrastructure. A CompositeResourceDefinition (XRD) defines what developers can ask for. A Composition defines what actually gets built. In Crossplane v2, composite resources are namespaced by default, so a developer's database lives in the service's own namespace, and the claim layer from v1 is gone.

The most important design decision is what you expose. Wrong:

# Leaky abstraction: developers now need to know RDS
spec:
  instanceClass: db.r6g.large
  allocatedStorage: 100
  engineVersion: "16.4"
  multiAz: true
  backupRetentionPeriod: 7
  dbSubnetGroupName: payflow-prod-private
  vpcSecurityGroupIds: ["sg-0d4f6a1b2c3e58790"]

spec:
  instanceClass: db.r6g.large

Right:

kind: CompositeResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: postgresdatabases.platform.payflow.io
spec:
  scope: Namespaced
  group: platform.payflow.io
  names:
    kind: PostgresDatabase
    plural: postgresdatabases
  versions:
    - name: v1alpha1
      served: true
      referenceable: true
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                size:
                  type: string
                  enum: [small, medium, large]
                  default: small
                highAvailability:
                  type: boolean
                  default: false

kind: PostgresDatabase

The Composition maps that intent onto real infrastructure. Subnets, security groups, encryption, backup retention, and the instance class are all decided by the platform team:

apiVersion: apiextensions.crossplane.io/v1
kind: Composition
metadata:
  name: postgres-aws
spec:
  compositeTypeRef:
    apiVersion: platform.payflow.io/v1alpha1
    kind: PostgresDatabase
  mode: Pipeline
  pipeline:
    - step: render-rds
      functionRef:
        name: function-patch-and-transform
      input:
        apiVersion: pt.fn.crossplane.io/v1beta1
        kind: Resources
        resources:
          - name: rds-instance
            base:
              apiVersion: rds.aws.m.upbound.io/v1beta1
              kind: Instance
              spec:
                managementPolicies: ["Observe", "Create", "Update", "LateInitialize"]
                forProvider:
                  region: ap-south-1
                  engine: postgres
                  engineVersion: "16"
                  allocatedStorage: 50
                  storageEncrypted: true
                  backupRetentionPeriod: 7
                  username: app_admin
                  manageMasterUserPassword: true
                  dbSubnetGroupName: payflow-prod-private
                  vpcSecurityGroupIds: ["sg-0d4f6a1b2c3e58790"]
                  skipFinalSnapshot: false
            patches:
              - type: FromCompositeFieldPath
                fromFieldPath: spec.size
                toFieldPath: spec.forProvider.instanceClass
                transforms:
                  - type: map
                    map:
                      small: db.t4g.medium
                      medium: db.r6g.large
                      large: db.r6g.2xlarge
              - type: FromCompositeFieldPath
                fromFieldPath: spec.highAvailability
                toFieldPath: spec.forProvider.multiAz
    - step: ready
      functionRef:
        name: function-auto-ready

metadata:

Two details are doing real work here. managementPolicies leaves out Delete, so even if the Kubernetes object disappears, the RDS instance stays in AWS. That's the second safeguard from the GitOps section. And manageMasterUserPassword puts the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager, where External Secrets Operator syncs them into the namespace. No password ever passes through Git or Backstage.

When the platform team later decides every database needs Performance Insights, they change one Composition. Every database picks up the change on its next reconcile, and no developer has to touch anything.

Golden Paths and Standardized Application Templates

A golden path is the supported, paved way to build a certain kind of thing. It isn't the only way. Teams with unusual needs can leave it, but then they own what they build. The goal is a path good enough that almost nobody wants to leave.

In this platform, the path for a service is a template plus a shared Helm chart. That pairing is what keeps it from rotting, and it's the mistake I see most often. Backstage templates run once. If the template copies 400 lines of Kubernetes manifests into each new repo, every service is frozen at the version it was born with. Fix a probe default in the template and none of your existing 40 services get the fix.

Keep the generated surface small and reference versioned platform artifacts instead. Here's everything a developer owns for their deployment:

# platform-gitops/apps/invoice-service/envs/production/values.yaml
service:
  name: invoice-service
  team: billing
  port: 8080
image:
  repository: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/invoice-service
  tag: 3f9c2a1
size: medium
autoscaling:
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 20
database:
  enabled: true
  size: medium
  highAvailability: true
# platform-gitops/apps/invoice-service/envs/production/values.yaml
service:
  name: invoice-service
  team: billing
  port: 8080
image:
  repository: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/invoice-service
  tag: 3f9c2a1
size: medium
autoscaling:
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 20
database:
  enabled: true
  size: medium
  highAvailability: true

From those 17 lines, the service chart renders a Deployment with sensible probes and security context, a Service, an HPA, a PodDisruptionBudget, a ServiceMonitor, an ExternalSecret for the database credentials, and the PostgresDatabase object. CI works the same way: the service repo calls a reusable workflow (payflow-eng/platform-workflows/.github/workflows/go-service.yml@v3) instead of carrying its own pipeline. When the platform team ships chart 2.5 or workflow v4, services adopt it with a version bump, and Renovate can open those PRs automatically.

Putting it together, here's what happens when a developer on the billing team needs a new service:

  1. They pick "Go Service (recommended)" in Backstage, enter invoice-service, choose the billing team, and select a small database.
  2. A repository is created with application code, a Dockerfile, catalog-info.yaml, and a CI workflow that calls the shared pipeline.
  3. A PR opens against platform-gitops with staging and production values. A platform reviewer (or an auto-merge rule for template-generated PRs) merges it.
  4. The ApplicationSet picks up the new directory, and Argo CD deploys the service to eks-staging.
  5. Crossplane provisions the RDS instance. About eight minutes later, its credentials land in the namespace as a Secret.
  6. Prometheus starts scraping through the generated ServiceMonitor, and the service page in Backstage shows Argo CD sync status, the Grafana dashboard, and the owning team.

The developer wrote zero Kubernetes manifests, didn't touch Terraform, and didn't file a ticket.

Security, RBAC, and Multi-Tenancy

Self-service only works if what developers can do is bounded. Here, the boundaries live in several layers so that no single one carries everything.

Every service gets its own namespace per environment, and the Argo CD services AppProject only allows namespaced resources from an approved list. A values file can't create a ClusterRole, because the project won't sync it. Developers get read access to their namespaces in production, and changes still go through Git.

Workload identity uses EKS Pod Identity, with the IAM role and association created by the same composition pattern, scoped to that service's resources. Secrets come from AWS Secrets Manager through External Secrets Operator. Nothing sensitive is stored in Git.

Kyverno enforces the rules the chart already follows, which catches anyone who leaves the golden path:

apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-team-label
spec:
  background: true
  rules:
    - name: check-team-label
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: [Deployment, StatefulSet]
      exclude:
        any:
          - resources:
              namespaces: [kube-system, argocd, crossplane-system]
      validate:
        failureAction: Enforce
        message: "Workloads need a 'team' label so alerts, costs, and ownership route to a real owner."
        pattern:
          metadata:
            labels:
              team: "?*"
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-team-label
spec:
  background: true
  rules:
    - name: check-team-label
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: [Deployment, StatefulSet]
      exclude:
        any:
          - resources:
              namespaces: [kube-system, argocd, crossplane-system]
      validate:
        failureAction: Enforce
        message: "Workloads need a 'team' label so alerts, costs, and ownership route to a real owner."
        pattern:
          metadata:
            labels:
              team: "?*"

The golden path passes this policy automatically. Teams that leave it find out at admission time, not during an incident.

Observability and Day-2 Operations

A platform that deploys services but leaves monitoring to each team has done half the job. Because the shared chart renders a ServiceMonitor, every service on the golden path exports metrics to Prometheus from its first deploy. Logs go to Loki with namespace, app, and team labels attached. A Grafana dashboard keyed on the service label works for every service without anyone building one.

The catalog is what ties it together. The generated catalog-info.yaml connects the service to its runtime:

apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: invoice-service
  annotations:
    argocd/app-name: invoice-service-production
    backstage.io/kubernetes-id: invoice-service
    grafana/dashboard-selector: "service=invoice-service"
    pagerduty.com/service-id: P7XK2QM
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  owner: group:billing
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: invoice-service
  annotations:
    argocd/app-name: invoice-service-production
    backstage.io/kubernetes-id: invoice-service
    grafana/dashboard-selector: "service=invoice-service"
    pagerduty.com/service-id: P7XK2QM
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  owner: group:billing

During an incident, an on-call engineer opens one page and sees the deployed version, sync status, Pods, dashboards, and who gets paged. Ownership also stops being tribal knowledge. The team label and catalog owner route alerts to billing, not to the platform team. The platform team owns the platform. Product teams own their services on it.

Common IDP Mistakes and Measuring Success

Building the portal first. Backstage on top of a platform that can't provision anything is a nice-looking catalog of tickets. Build the golden path end to end with Git, Argo CD, and Crossplane first. The portal is the last mile.

Abstracting too much. If your PostgresDatabase API has no way to set max_connections, the first team that needs it will leave the platform entirely. Keep a documented escape hatch, for example an optional parameters map that only the platform team's policy allows in specific namespaces.

Mandating adoption instead of earning it. Teams forced onto a slow platform route around it quietly. If the golden path isn't the fastest way to ship, fix the path.

Treating the platform as a project. Templates, charts, and compositions need versioning, changelogs, and deprecation windows, the same as any product your customers depend on. Your customers here just happen to sit in the same Slack.

Measure the platform the way you'd measure a product. These are the numbers I track:

IDP readiness checklist

  • Git is the only write path; the portal creates PRs, not resources
  • One ApplicationSet onboards services from directory structure
  • preserveResourcesOnDeletion is set, and production cloud resources exclude Delete from managementPolicies
  • Crossplane XRDs expose intent (size: small), not provider fields
  • Templates generate a thin values file and reference a versioned shared chart and CI workflow
  • Argo CD AppProjects restrict which resource kinds teams can deploy
  • Kyverno enforces the same rules the golden path already follows
  • Every service ships with metrics, logs, a dashboard, and an owner from day one
  • Platform metrics are tracked and reviewed like product metrics

A good internal developer platform is measured by how little a developer needs to know to use it well. Kubernetes didn't get simpler in this design. The complexity moved to a team that's paid to own it, behind APIs that say size: small instead of db.t4g.medium. Every field you remove from a developer's view is a decision your platform team made once so forty teams don't have to make it badly.

Tom Jose is a DevOps Engineer at KotaiCode, where the team helps companies get their Kubernetes and AWS infrastructure production-ready.

On most clusters I review, the answer lands between 12 and 20. A Deployment, a Service, an Ingress, an HPA, a ServiceAccount, an IAM role, a Terraform module for the database, an ExternalSecret, a ServiceMonitor, a GitHub Actions workflow, an Argo CD Application, and then a Jira ticket to the platform team for whatever's left.
Almost none of those files describe the service. They describe the infrastructure around it. Developers end up copying manifests from a neighbouring repo, changing the names, and hoping. Six months later you have forty services with forty slightly different ways of doing health checks.
This article walks through an Internal Developer Platform (IDP) built from Backstage, Argo CD, and Crossplane on EKS. In it, a developer goes from "I need a new service with a Postgres database" to a running, monitored deployment without writing a Kubernetes manifest or opening the AWS console. It's an architecture article, so there are no installation steps.
Why Kubernetes Alone Isn't a Developer Platform
Kubernetes gives you primitives: Pods, Services, volumes, RBAC. Primitives are what you build a platform from. They aren't a platform themselves. Handing raw Kubernetes to product teams creates three problems that get worse as you grow.
The first is cognitive load. A developer who wants to add a queue consumer shouldn't need to understand IRSA trust policies or why maxUnavailable: 0 matters during a rollout. Every hour spent on that is an hour not spent on the product.
The second is inconsistency. When every team writes its own manifests, every team makes its own mistakes. One service has no resource requests, another runs as root, a third has no PodDisruptionBudget. You find out which one during an incident.
The third is the ticket queue. Infrastructure that Kubernetes can't provision (databases, buckets, IAM) usually goes through the platform team. The team becomes a bottleneck, so developers wait days for an RDS instance that Terraform creates in eight minutes.
An IDP fixes all three by changing what developers interact with. They stop working with infrastructure and start working with products the platform team builds: a service template, a database API, a deployment workflow. The YAML still exists. It just moves to the people whose job is maintaining it.
Designing the Internal Developer Platform Architecture
Here's the architecture this article builds. Each layer has one job, and developers only touch the top one.

  
  
  

The design principle that matters most is that Git is the only write path. Backstage never calls the Kubernetes API or AWS directly. It creates repositories and opens pull requests. Argo CD reconciles what's in Git, and Crossplane reconciles cloud resources from Kubernetes objects that Argo CD applied.
That means every change, including "create a database," is reviewable, auditable, and revertable with the same tools. It also means Backstage can go down without taking deployments with it. The portal is a front door, not a dependency.
Building a Self-Service Developer Portal
Backstage does three jobs in this setup. The service catalog answers "who owns this and where does it run." TechDocs keeps documentation next to the code. Software templates create new things. The templates are where the self-service happens.
A template is a form plus a sequence of actions. Here's a trimmed version of the golden path template for a Go service with an optional database:

						
							
							apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: go-service
  title: Go Service (recommended)
  description: HTTP service with CI, GitOps deployment, monitoring, and optional Postgres
  tags: [go, recommended]
spec:
  owner: group:platform-team
  type: service
  parameters:
    - title: Service details
      required: [name, owner]
      properties:
        name:
          title: Service name
          type: string
          pattern: '^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{2,30}$'
        owner:
          title: Owning team
          type: string
          ui:field: OwnerPicker
          ui:options:
            catalogFilter:
              kind: Group
        database:
          title: Postgres database
          type: string
          enum: [none, small, medium]
          default: none
  steps:
    - id: fetch-service
      name: Generate service code
      action: fetch:template
      input:
        url: ./skeleton
        values:
          name: ${{ parameters.name }}
          owner: ${{ parameters.owner }}
    - id: publish
      name: Create GitHub repository
      action: publish:github
      input:
        repoUrl: github.com?owner=payflow-eng&repo=${{ parameters.name }}
        defaultBranch: main
        protectDefaultBranch: true
    - id: fetch-gitops
      name: Generate deployment config
      action: fetch:template
      input:
        url: ./gitops
        targetPath: ./gitops
        values:
          name: ${{ parameters.name }}
          owner: ${{ parameters.owner }}
          database: ${{ parameters.database }}
    - id: gitops-pr
      name: Open GitOps pull request
      action: publish:github:pull-request
      input:
        repoUrl: github.com?owner=payflow-eng&repo=platform-gitops
        branchName: onboard-${{ parameters.name }}
        title: "Onboard ${{ parameters.name }}"
        description: Generated by the go-service template
        sourcePath: ./gitops
        targetPath: apps/${{ parameters.name }}
    - id: register
      name: Register in catalog
      action: catalog:register
      input:
        repoContentsUrl: ${{ steps['publish'].output.repoContentsUrl }}
        catalogInfoPath: /catalog-info.yaml
  output:
    links:
      - title: Repository
        url: ${{ steps['publish'].output.remoteUrl }}
      - title: Deployment pull request
        url: ${{ steps['gitops-pr'].output.remoteUrl }}

The developer fills in three fields. The template creates the repository, opens the deployment PR, and registers the service in the catalog with its owner attached.
Notice the database field is an enum with three values, not a free-text instance class. That's deliberate, and it comes back in the Crossplane section.
GitOps as the Deployment Engine
Argo CD is the deployment engine, and the platform-gitops repository is its single source of truth. The layout is boring on purpose:

						
							
							platform-gitops/
  apps/
    invoice-service/
      envs/
        staging/values.yaml
        production/values.yaml
    ledger-api/
      envs/
        staging/values.yaml
        production/values.yaml
							platform-gitops/
  apps/
    invoice-service/
      envs/
        staging/values.yaml
        production/values.yaml
    ledger-api/
      envs/
        staging/values.yaml
        production/values.yaml
						
					
One ApplicationSet turns every apps/*/envs/* directory into an Argo CD Application, so onboarding a service means merging a PR. Nobody writes an Application by hand:

						
							
							apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: services
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  goTemplate: true
  goTemplateOptions: ["missingkey=error"]
  generators:
    - git:
        repoURL: https://github.com/payflow-eng/platform-gitops.git
        revision: main
        directories:
          - path: apps/*/envs/*
  syncPolicy:
    preserveResourcesOnDeletion: true
  template:
    metadata:
      name: '{{index .path.segments 1}}-{{.path.basename}}'
    spec:
      project: services
      sources:
        - repoURL: https://github.com/payflow-eng/platform-charts.git
          targetRevision: service-chart-2.4.1
          path: charts/service
          helm:
            valueFiles:
              - $values/{{.path.path}}/values.yaml
        - repoURL: https://github.com/payflow-eng/platform-gitops.git
          targetRevision: main
          ref: values
      destination:
        name: 'eks-{{.path.basename}}'
        namespace: '{{index .path.segments 1}}'
      syncPolicy:
        automated:
          prune: true
          selfHeal: true
        syncOptions:
          - CreateNamespace=true
							apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: services
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  goTemplate: true
  goTemplateOptions: ["missingkey=error"]
  generators:
    - git:
        repoURL: https://github.com/payflow-eng/platform-gitops.git
        revision: main
        directories:
          - path: apps/*/envs/*
  syncPolicy:
    preserveResourcesOnDeletion: true
  template:
    metadata:
      name: '{{index .path.segments 1}}-{{.path.basename}}'
    spec:
      project: services
      sources:
        - repoURL: https://github.com/payflow-eng/platform-charts.git
          targetRevision: service-chart-2.4.1
          path: charts/service
          helm:
            valueFiles:
              - $values/{{.path.path}}/values.yaml
        - repoURL: https://github.com/payflow-eng/platform-gitops.git
          targetRevision: main
          ref: values
      destination:
        name: 'eks-{{.path.basename}}'
        namespace: '{{index .path.segments 1}}'
      syncPolicy:
        automated:
          prune: true
          selfHeal: true
        syncOptions:
          - CreateNamespace=true
						
					
Each environment maps to a cluster (eks-staging, eks-production) registered in Argo CD. CI in the service repo builds the image, pushes it to ECR, and opens a PR that bumps the tag in staging/values.yaml. Promotion to production is another PR that copies the same tag forward. Git history becomes the deployment log.
Here's the sharp edge almost nobody plans for. That ApplicationSet also deploys the service's PostgresDatabase object. If someone deletes apps/invoice-service/ in a cleanup PR, the default behavior cascades: the Application is deleted, its resources are pruned, Crossplane sees the database object disappear, and it deletes the RDS instance. That's why preserveResourcesOnDeletion: true is in the manifest above. The Crossplane section adds a second safeguard, because one layer of protection on production data isn't enough.
Self-Service Infrastructure with Crossplane
Crossplane lets the platform team define its own Kubernetes APIs for cloud infrastructure. A CompositeResourceDefinition (XRD) defines what developers can ask for. A Composition defines what actually gets built. In Crossplane v2, composite resources are namespaced by default, so a developer's database lives in the service's own namespace, and the claim layer from v1 is gone.
The most important design decision is what you expose. Wrong:

						
							
							# Leaky abstraction: developers now need to know RDS
spec:
  instanceClass: db.r6g.large
  allocatedStorage: 100
  engineVersion: "16.4"
  multiAz: true
  backupRetentionPeriod: 7
  dbSubnetGroupName: payflow-prod-private
  vpcSecurityGroupIds: ["sg-0d4f6a1b2c3e58790"]
							# Leaky abstraction: developers now need to know RDS
spec:
  instanceClass: db.r6g.large
  allocatedStorage: 100
  engineVersion: "16.4"
  multiAz: true
  backupRetentionPeriod: 7
  dbSubnetGroupName: payflow-prod-private
  vpcSecurityGroupIds: ["sg-0d4f6a1b2c3e58790"]
						
					
Right:

						
							
							apiVersion: apiextensions.crossplane.io/v2
kind: CompositeResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: postgresdatabases.platform.payflow.io
spec:
  scope: Namespaced
  group: platform.payflow.io
  names:
    kind: PostgresDatabase
    plural: postgresdatabases
  versions:
    - name: v1alpha1
      served: true
      referenceable: true
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                size:
                  type: string
                  enum: [small, medium, large]
                  default: small
                highAvailability:
                  type: boolean
                  default: false
							apiVersion: apiextensions.crossplane.io/v2
kind: CompositeResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: postgresdatabases.platform.payflow.io
spec:
  scope: Namespaced
  group: platform.payflow.io
  names:
    kind: PostgresDatabase
    plural: postgresdatabases
  versions:
    - name: v1alpha1
      served: true
      referenceable: true
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                size:
                  type: string
                  enum: [small, medium, large]
                  default: small
                highAvailability:
                  type: boolean
                  default: false
						
					
The developer's entire request is this:

						
							
							apiVersion: platform.payflow.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresDatabase
metadata:
  name: invoice-db
  namespace: invoice-service
spec:
  size: small
							apiVersion: platform.payflow.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresDatabase
metadata:
  name: invoice-db
  namespace: invoice-service
spec:
  size: small
						
					
The Composition maps that intent onto real infrastructure. Subnets, security groups, encryption, backup retention, and the instance class are all decided by the platform team:

						
							
							apiVersion: apiextensions.crossplane.io/v1
kind: Composition
metadata:
  name: postgres-aws
spec:
  compositeTypeRef:
    apiVersion: platform.payflow.io/v1alpha1
    kind: PostgresDatabase
  mode: Pipeline
  pipeline:
    - step: render-rds
      functionRef:
        name: function-patch-and-transform
      input:
        apiVersion: pt.fn.crossplane.io/v1beta1
        kind: Resources
        resources:
          - name: rds-instance
            base:
              apiVersion: rds.aws.m.upbound.io/v1beta1
              kind: Instance
              spec:
                managementPolicies: ["Observe", "Create", "Update", "LateInitialize"]
                forProvider:
                  region: ap-south-1
                  engine: postgres
                  engineVersion: "16"
                  allocatedStorage: 50
                  storageEncrypted: true
                  backupRetentionPeriod: 7
                  username: app_admin
                  manageMasterUserPassword: true
                  dbSubnetGroupName: payflow-prod-private
                  vpcSecurityGroupIds: ["sg-0d4f6a1b2c3e58790"]
                  skipFinalSnapshot: false
            patches:
              - type: FromCompositeFieldPath
                fromFieldPath: spec.size
                toFieldPath: spec.forProvider.instanceClass
                transforms:
                  - type: map
                    map:
                      small: db.t4g.medium
                      medium: db.r6g.large
                      large: db.r6g.2xlarge
              - type: FromCompositeFieldPath
                fromFieldPath: spec.highAvailability
                toFieldPath: spec.forProvider.multiAz
    - step: ready
      functionRef:
        name: function-auto-ready
							apiVersion: apiextensions.crossplane.io/v1
kind: Composition
metadata:
  name: postgres-aws
spec:
  compositeTypeRef:
    apiVersion: platform.payflow.io/v1alpha1
    kind: PostgresDatabase
  mode: Pipeline
  pipeline:
    - step: render-rds
      functionRef:
        name: function-patch-and-transform
      input:
        apiVersion: pt.fn.crossplane.io/v1beta1
        kind: Resources
        resources:
          - name: rds-instance
            base:
              apiVersion: rds.aws.m.upbound.io/v1beta1
              kind: Instance
              spec:
                managementPolicies: ["Observe", "Create", "Update", "LateInitialize"]
                forProvider:
                  region: ap-south-1
                  engine: postgres
                  engineVersion: "16"
                  allocatedStorage: 50
                  storageEncrypted: true
                  backupRetentionPeriod: 7
                  username: app_admin
                  manageMasterUserPassword: true
                  dbSubnetGroupName: payflow-prod-private
                  vpcSecurityGroupIds: ["sg-0d4f6a1b2c3e58790"]
                  skipFinalSnapshot: false
            patches:
              - type: FromCompositeFieldPath
                fromFieldPath: spec.size
                toFieldPath: spec.forProvider.instanceClass
                transforms:
                  - type: map
                    map:
                      small: db.t4g.medium
                      medium: db.r6g.large
                      large: db.r6g.2xlarge
              - type: FromCompositeFieldPath
                fromFieldPath: spec.highAvailability
                toFieldPath: spec.forProvider.multiAz
    - step: ready
      functionRef:
        name: function-auto-ready
						
					
Two details are doing real work here. managementPolicies leaves out Delete, so even if the Kubernetes object disappears, the RDS instance stays in AWS. That's the second safeguard from the GitOps section. And manageMasterUserPassword puts the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager, where External Secrets Operator syncs them into the namespace. No password ever passes through Git or Backstage.
When the platform team later decides every database needs Performance Insights, they change one Composition. Every database picks up the change on its next reconcile, and no developer has to touch anything.
Golden Paths and Standardized Application Templates
A golden path is the supported, paved way to build a certain kind of thing. It isn't the only way. Teams with unusual needs can leave it, but then they own what they build. The goal is a path good enough that almost nobody wants to leave.
In this platform, the path for a service is a template plus a shared Helm chart. That pairing is what keeps it from rotting, and it's the mistake I see most often. Backstage templates run once. If the template copies 400 lines of Kubernetes manifests into each new repo, every service is frozen at the version it was born with. Fix a probe default in the template and none of your existing 40 services get the fix.
Keep the generated surface small and reference versioned platform artifacts instead. Here's everything a developer owns for their deployment:

						
							
							# platform-gitops/apps/invoice-service/envs/production/values.yaml
service:
  name: invoice-service
  team: billing
  port: 8080
image:
  repository: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/invoice-service
  tag: 3f9c2a1
size: medium
autoscaling:
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 20
database:
  enabled: true
  size: medium
  highAvailability: true
							# platform-gitops/apps/invoice-service/envs/production/values.yaml
service:
  name: invoice-service
  team: billing
  port: 8080
image:
  repository: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/invoice-service
  tag: 3f9c2a1
size: medium
autoscaling:
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 20
database:
  enabled: true
  size: medium
  highAvailability: true
						
					
From those 17 lines, the service chart renders a Deployment with sensible probes and security context, a Service, an HPA, a PodDisruptionBudget, a ServiceMonitor, an ExternalSecret for the database credentials, and the PostgresDatabase object. CI works the same way: the service repo calls a reusable workflow (payflow-eng/platform-workflows/.github/workflows/go-service.yml@v3) instead of carrying its own pipeline. When the platform team ships chart 2.5 or workflow v4, services adopt it with a version bump, and Renovate can open those PRs automatically.
Putting it together, here's what happens when a developer on the billing team needs a new service:

They pick "Go Service (recommended)" in Backstage, enter invoice-service, choose the billing team, and select a small database.
A repository is created with application code, a Dockerfile, catalog-info.yaml, and a CI workflow that calls the shared pipeline.
A PR opens against platform-gitops with staging and production values. A platform reviewer (or an auto-merge rule for template-generated PRs) merges it.
The ApplicationSet picks up the new directory, and Argo CD deploys the service to eks-staging.
Crossplane provisions the RDS instance. About eight minutes later, its credentials land in the namespace as a Secret.
Prometheus starts scraping through the generated ServiceMonitor, and the service page in Backstage shows Argo CD sync status, the Grafana dashboard, and the owning team.

The developer wrote zero Kubernetes manifests, didn't touch Terraform, and didn't file a ticket.
Security, RBAC, and Multi-Tenancy
Self-service only works if what developers can do is bounded. Here, the boundaries live in several layers so that no single one carries everything.
Every service gets its own namespace per environment, and the Argo CD services AppProject only allows namespaced resources from an approved list. A values file can't create a ClusterRole, because the project won't sync it. Developers get read access to their namespaces in production, and changes still go through Git.
Workload identity uses EKS Pod Identity, with the IAM role and association created by the same composition pattern, scoped to that service's resources. Secrets come from AWS Secrets Manager through External Secrets Operator. Nothing sensitive is stored in Git.
Kyverno enforces the rules the chart already follows, which catches anyone who leaves the golden path:

						
							
							apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-team-label
spec:
  background: true
  rules:
    - name: check-team-label
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: [Deployment, StatefulSet]
      exclude:
        any:
          - resources:
              namespaces: [kube-system, argocd, crossplane-system]
      validate:
        failureAction: Enforce
        message: "Workloads need a 'team' label so alerts, costs, and ownership route to a real owner."
        pattern:
          metadata:
            labels:
              team: "?*"
							apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-team-label
spec:
  background: true
  rules:
    - name: check-team-label
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: [Deployment, StatefulSet]
      exclude:
        any:
          - resources:
              namespaces: [kube-system, argocd, crossplane-system]
      validate:
        failureAction: Enforce
        message: "Workloads need a 'team' label so alerts, costs, and ownership route to a real owner."
        pattern:
          metadata:
            labels:
              team: "?*"
						
					
The golden path passes this policy automatically. Teams that leave it find out at admission time, not during an incident.
Observability and Day-2 Operations
A platform that deploys services but leaves monitoring to each team has done half the job. Because the shared chart renders a ServiceMonitor, every service on the golden path exports metrics to Prometheus from its first deploy. Logs go to Loki with namespace, app, and team labels attached. A Grafana dashboard keyed on the service label works for every service without anyone building one.
The catalog is what ties it together. The generated catalog-info.yaml connects the service to its runtime:

						
							
							apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: invoice-service
  annotations:
    argocd/app-name: invoice-service-production
    backstage.io/kubernetes-id: invoice-service
    grafana/dashboard-selector: "service=invoice-service"
    pagerduty.com/service-id: P7XK2QM
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  owner: group:billing
							apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: invoice-service
  annotations:
    argocd/app-name: invoice-service-production
    backstage.io/kubernetes-id: invoice-service
    grafana/dashboard-selector: "service=invoice-service"
    pagerduty.com/service-id: P7XK2QM
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  owner: group:billing
						
					
During an incident, an on-call engineer opens one page and sees the deployed version, sync status, Pods, dashboards, and who gets paged. Ownership also stops being tribal knowledge. The team label and catalog owner route alerts to billing, not to the platform team. The platform team owns the platform. Product teams own their services on it.
Common IDP Mistakes and Measuring Success
Building the portal first. Backstage on top of a platform that can't provision anything is a nice-looking catalog of tickets. Build the golden path end to end with Git, Argo CD, and Crossplane first. The portal is the last mile.
Abstracting too much. If your PostgresDatabase API has no way to set max_connections, the first team that needs it will leave the platform entirely. Keep a documented escape hatch, for example an optional parameters map that only the platform team's policy allows in specific namespaces.
Mandating adoption instead of earning it. Teams forced onto a slow platform route around it quietly. If the golden path isn't the fastest way to ship, fix the path.
Treating the platform as a project. Templates, charts, and compositions need versioning, changelogs, and deprecation windows, the same as any product your customers depend on. Your customers here just happen to sit in the same Slack.
Measure the platform the way you'd measure a product. These are the numbers I track:

  
  
  

IDP readiness checklist

Git is the only write path; the portal creates PRs, not resources
One ApplicationSet onboards services from directory structure
preserveResourcesOnDeletion is set, and production cloud resources exclude Delete from managementPolicies
Crossplane XRDs expose intent (size: small), not provider fields
Templates generate a thin values file and reference a versioned shared chart and CI workflow
Argo CD AppProjects restrict which resource kinds teams can deploy
Kyverno enforces the same rules the golden path already follows
Every service ships with metrics, logs, a dashboard, and an owner from day one
Platform metrics are tracked and reviewed like product metrics

A good internal developer platform is measured by how little a developer needs to know to use it well. Kubernetes didn't get simpler in this design. The complexity moved to a team that's paid to own it, behind APIs that say size: small instead of db.t4g.medium. Every field you remove from a developer's view is a decision your platform team made once so forty teams don't have to make it badly.
Tom Jose is a DevOps Engineer at KotaiCode, where the team helps companies get their Kubernetes and AWS infrastructure production-ready.

June 12, 2026

Top 7 MCP Servers for AWS Infrastructure Automation

AWS is where most engineering organisations’ infrastructure lives, and AWS is increasingly where AI automation delivers the most immediate…

By Neel Shah

7 min read

  • 1 The 7 AWS MCP Servers
  • 2 1 AWS Labs MCP Server (Official) — The comprehensive, official AWS MCP implementation
  • 3 2 CloudWatch MCP Server — Metrics, alarms, logs, and observability queries
  • 4 3 AWS Cost Explorer MCP Server — Cloud cost analysis, recommendations, and forecasting
  • 5 4 AWS IAM MCP Server — IAM inspection, policy analysis, and access investigation
  • 6 5 Amazon EKS MCP Server — EKS cluster management and Kubernetes-AWS integration
  • 7 6 AWS CloudTrail MCP Server — API audit logs, compliance investigation, and change tracking
  • 8 7 AWS Systems Manager MCP Server — SSM Parameter Store, Run Command, and fleet management
  • 9 Multi-Server AWS Workflows
  • 10 Workflow 2: Automated FinOps Weekly Review
  • 11 Workflow 3: Incident Root Cause via CloudTrail

AWS is where most engineering organisations' infrastructure lives, and AWS is increasingly where AI automation delivers the most immediate ROI. The challenge has always been the complexity of the AWS API surface: EC2, RDS, ECS, EKS, Lambda, S3, IAM, CloudWatch, CloudTrail, Cost Explorer, and hundreds of other services each have their own SDKs, CLI syntax, and console navigation patterns. Even experienced AWS engineers spend significant time on the mechanical work of cross-referencing state across services, constructing CLI queries, and navigating the console.

MCP servers for AWS change this. Instead of running aws ec2 describe-instances with the correct — filters syntax, you ask your AI assistant a question in natural language and the MCP server translates it to the correct API call, executes it, and returns the result in context-aware format. Instead of switching between the EC2 console, CloudWatch, CloudTrail, and Cost Explorer to diagnose a cost spike, you ask a single question and the AI queries all four simultaneously.

This guide covers the seven most valuable MCP servers for AWS infrastructure teams in 2026. We go beyond installation instructions to cover the specific workflows each server enables, the IAM permission design you should implement, and the combination patterns that unlock the most powerful multi-service automation.

SECURITY-FIRST NOTE

Every MCP server described in this guide should run with a dedicated IAM role or user with the minimum permissions required for its use cases. Never share credentials between MCP servers. Rotate credentials quarterly. Enable CloudTrail logging and review AI-generated API calls regularly — you are accountable for what runs under your credentials, regardless of whether a human or an AI made the call.

IAM Foundation: Before You Connect Any MCP Server

The right IAM architecture for AWS MCP servers uses dedicated IAM identities with separate permission scopes for investigative (read) and automation (write) use cases. This is not optional — it is the foundation that makes AI-assisted AWS automation safe to run in production.

Terraform: IAM role for read-only AWS MCP investigation

resource "aws_iam_role" "mcp_readonly" {

name = "mcp-ai-readonly"

assume_role_policy = jsonencode({

Version = "2012–10–17"

Statement = [{

Effect = "Allow"

Principal = { AWS = "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:root" }

Action = "sts:AssumeRole"

Condition = {

StringEquals = {

"aws:PrincipalTag/MCPRole" = "true"

}

}

}]

})

}

resource "aws_iam_role_policy_attachment" "mcp_readonly" {

role = aws_iam_role.mcp_readonly.name

policy_arn = "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/ReadOnlyAccess"

}

Additional cost explorer permission (not in ReadOnlyAccess):

resource "aws_iam_role_policy" "cost_explorer" {

role = aws_iam_role.mcp_readonly.name

policy = jsonencode({

Version = "2012–10–17"

Statement = [{

Effect = "Allow"

Action = ["ce:GetCostAndUsage", "ce:GetRecommendations",

"ce:GetCostForecast", "ce:ListCostAllocationTags"]

Resource = "*"

}]

})

}

The 7 AWS MCP Servers

1 AWS Labs MCP Server (Official) — The comprehensive, official AWS MCP implementation

Maintained By

AWS Labs (github.com/awslabs/mcp) — official Amazon-maintained

Coverage

EC2, S3, EKS, ECS, Lambda, IAM, CloudFormation, CloudWatch, RDS, ElastiCache and growing

Install

pip install awslabs-mcp-server OR uvx awslabs.mcp

Auth

Standard AWS credential chain: env vars, ~/.aws/credentials, instance role, or assumed role

Killer Feature

Natural language AWS CLI: ask 'which EC2 instances in us-east-1 have been running more than 90 days and have average CPU below 3%?' — gets structured, actionable results

2026 Status

Active development; new service coverage added monthly; use this as your primary AWS MCP

The AWS Labs MCP server covers the broadest surface area and has the most active maintenance cadence. For most AWS operations, start here. The natural language to API translation handles the most common query patterns well: resource listing with filters, cross-service tagging searches, resource utilization queries, and configuration inspection.

Configuration for Claude Desktop:

{

"mcpServers": {

"aws": {

"command": "uvx",

"args": ["awslabs.mcp-server"],

"env": {

"AWS_PROFILE": "mcp-readonly",

"AWS_REGION": "us-east-1",

"AWS_DEFAULT_REGION": "us-east-1"

}

}

}

}

Sample questions the AI can now answer:

'List all S3 buckets that have public access enabled'

'Show me all RDS instances not in a Multi-AZ configuration'

'Which Lambda functions have not been invoked in the last 30 days?'

'Find all security groups that allow 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22'

2 CloudWatch MCP Server — Metrics, alarms, logs, and observability queries

Maintained By

Community: github.com/aws-cloudwatch-mcp (most maintained fork)

Coverage

CloudWatch Metrics, Alarms, Log Insights, Contributor Insights, ServiceLens

Install

npm install -g mcp-server-cloudwatch

Key Tools

query_metrics, run_log_insights, list_alarms, get_alarm_history, get_anomaly_detector

Killer Workflow

'Run a Log Insights query across all Lambda function logs in the last 24 hours and show me all ERROR patterns with their frequency and first occurrence'

IAM Permissions

cloudwatch:GetMetricData, cloudwatch:DescribeAlarms, logs:StartQuery, logs:GetQueryResults, logs:FilterLogEvents

CloudWatch Log Insights via MCP — what you can now ask:

'Find all 5xx errors in the payments-api log group in the last 2 hours'

'Show me the top 10 slowest Lambda invocations this week with their trace IDs'

'Are there any alarms currently in ALARM state across all regions?'

'Query the VPC flow logs for any traffic denied to the database subnet group'

Log Insights query the AI generates and executes:

fields @timestamp, @message, @logStream

| filter @message like /ERROR/

| stats count(*) as error_count by bin(5m)

| sort error_count desc

| limit 20

3 AWS Cost Explorer MCP Server — Cloud cost analysis, recommendations, and forecasting

Maintained By

Community + AWS SDK wrapper: github.com/aws-cost-mcp

Coverage

Cost and Usage Reports, Savings Plans, Reserved Instance recommendations, Cost Anomaly Detection

Install

pip install aws-cost-mcp-server

Key Tools

get_cost_by_service, get_cost_anomalies, get_savings_plan_recommendations, get_ri_utilization, get_cost_forecast

Killer Workflow

'Which teams have exceeded their monthly cloud budget, broken down by service, compared to last month?'

IAM Permissions

ce:GetCostAndUsage, ce:GetRecommendations, ce:GetCostForecast, ce:GetAnomalies (all read-only)

Best Use

Monthly FinOps review: 'Summarise this month's AWS spend vs. last month, flag any anomalies, and list the top 3 cost reduction opportunities'

4 AWS IAM MCP Server — IAM inspection, policy analysis, and access investigation

Maintained By

Community: github.com/iam-mcp-server

Coverage

IAM Users, Roles, Policies, Access Advisor, Credential Reports, Permission Boundaries

Install

uvx iam-mcp-server

Key Tools

list_roles, get_role_policies, get_access_advisor, generate_credential_report, simulate_policy, find_unused_permissions

Killer Workflow

'Which IAM roles have admin-equivalent permissions but have not been used in the last 90 days?'

IAM Permissions

iam:Get*, iam:List*, iam:GenerateCredentialReport, iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy

Security Value

June 12, 2026 Top 7 MCP Servers for AWS Infrastructure Automation AWS is where most engineering organisations’ infrastructure lives, and AWS is increasingly where AI automation delivers the most immediate…  By Neel Shah 7 min read     1 The 7 AWS MCP Servers2 1 AWS Labs MCP Server (Official) — The comprehensive, official AWS MCP implementation3 2 CloudWatch MCP Server — Metrics, alarms, logs, and observability queries4 3 AWS Cost Explorer MCP Server — Cloud cost analysis, recommendations, and forecasting5 4 AWS IAM MCP Server — IAM inspection, policy analysis, and access investigation6 5 Amazon EKS MCP Server — EKS cluster management and Kubernetes-AWS integration7 6 AWS CloudTrail MCP Server — API audit logs, compliance investigation, and change tracking8 7 AWS Systems Manager MCP Server — SSM Parameter Store, Run Command, and fleet management9 Multi-Server AWS Workflows10 Workflow 2: Automated FinOps Weekly Review11 Workflow 3: Incident Root Cause via CloudTrail  AWS is where most engineering organisations' infrastructure lives, and AWS is increasingly where AI automation delivers the most immediate ROI. The challenge has always been the complexity of the AWS API surface: EC2, RDS, ECS, EKS, Lambda, S3, IAM, CloudWatch, CloudTrail, Cost Explorer, and hundreds of other services each have their own SDKs, CLI syntax, and console navigation patterns. Even experienced AWS engineers spend significant time on the mechanical work of cross-referencing state across services, constructing CLI queries, and navigating the console.
MCP servers for AWS change this. Instead of running aws ec2 describe-instances with the correct — filters syntax, you ask your AI assistant a question in natural language and the MCP server translates it to the correct API call, executes it, and returns the result in context-aware format. Instead of switching between the EC2 console, CloudWatch, CloudTrail, and Cost Explorer to diagnose a cost spike, you ask a single question and the AI queries all four simultaneously.
This guide covers the seven most valuable MCP servers for AWS infrastructure teams in 2026. We go beyond installation instructions to cover the specific workflows each server enables, the IAM permission design you should implement, and the combination patterns that unlock the most powerful multi-service automation.
SECURITY-FIRST NOTE
Every MCP server described in this guide should run with a dedicated IAM role or user with the minimum permissions required for its use cases. Never share credentials between MCP servers. Rotate credentials quarterly. Enable CloudTrail logging and review AI-generated API calls regularly — you are accountable for what runs under your credentials, regardless of whether a human or an AI made the call.
IAM Foundation: Before You Connect Any MCP Server
The right IAM architecture for AWS MCP servers uses dedicated IAM identities with separate permission scopes for investigative (read) and automation (write) use cases. This is not optional — it is the foundation that makes AI-assisted AWS automation safe to run in production.
Terraform: IAM role for read-only AWS MCP investigation
resource "aws_iam_role" "mcp_readonly" {
name = "mcp-ai-readonly"
assume_role_policy = jsonencode({
Version = "2012–10–17"
Statement = [{
Effect = "Allow"
Principal = { AWS = "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:root" }
Action = "sts:AssumeRole"
Condition = {
StringEquals = {
"aws:PrincipalTag/MCPRole" = "true"
}
}
}]
})
}
resource "aws_iam_role_policy_attachment" "mcp_readonly" {
role = aws_iam_role.mcp_readonly.name
policy_arn = "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/ReadOnlyAccess"
}
Additional cost explorer permission (not in ReadOnlyAccess):
resource "aws_iam_role_policy" "cost_explorer" {
role = aws_iam_role.mcp_readonly.name
policy = jsonencode({
Version = "2012–10–17"
Statement = [{
Effect = "Allow"
Action = ["ce:GetCostAndUsage", "ce:GetRecommendations",
"ce:GetCostForecast", "ce:ListCostAllocationTags"]
Resource = "*"
}]
})
}

Active development; new service coverage added monthly; use this as your primary AWS MCP
The AWS Labs MCP server covers the broadest surface area and has the most active maintenance cadence. For most AWS operations, start here.
